pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Rainforest Animals (ages 7–9): the most species-rich habitat on Earth, structured in vertical LAYERS (forest floor, understory, canopy, emergent) each home to different animals with layer-matched adaptations.
• Standards — UK (DfE): extends KS1 'Living things and their habitats' and Y4 grouping/adaptation; the layer structure introduces the idea that ONE habitat contains many micro-environments.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 2-LS4-1 ([curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS4-1] different places); 3-LS4-3 (survival in a habitat) — rainforest biodiversity is the flagship case of 'many kinds in one place'.
• Operational details: anchor the four layers with signature animals and layer-linked adaptations — canopy (howler monkeys, sloths, toucans, tree frogs: gripping hands/tails, gliding, bright colours); understory (jaguars climbing, snakes, insects: camouflage, ambush); forest floor (tapirs, ants, decomposers: foraging, burrowing); emergent (harpy eagle, large birds/bats: flight above the trees). Establish that rainforests grow near the equator, are warm and wet all year, and hold more species than any other land habitat.
• Checkpoint — A (concrete, ~7–8): name the layers and one animal in each. B (transitional, ~8–9): explain one adaptation that suits an animal to its layer (e.g. prehensile tail for canopy life). C (formal, ~9): explain WHY rainforests hold so many species (warm, wet, year-round, many niches/layers).
bestPractices: Teach the forest as a vertical stack, not a flat scene — build the four layers bottom-to-top so pupils grasp light and food changing with height and animals matched to each level.
Tie each adaptation to its layer's demand (prehensile tails and gripping feet for the canopy; camouflage and ambush for the dim understory; decomposing/foraging on the floor).
Use the biodiversity hook concretely — 'a single rainforest tree can hold more ant species than the whole UK' — to make 'most species-rich' vivid rather than abstract.
Connect to warmth-and-water availability so pupils reason about WHY so much life is possible here, linking back to what plants/animals need.
keyRepresentations: A cross-section of the rainforest showing the four stacked layers with signature animals placed in each.
A light gradient down the layers (bright emergent → dark floor) explaining why canopy life differs from floor life.
Adaptation close-ups: a prehensile tail gripping a branch, a sloth's hook-like claws, a tree frog's sticky toe pads.
A 'species pile-up' comparison bar: rainforest vs other habitats to show sheer diversity.
commonMisconceptions: 'The rainforest floor is where most animals live' — the canopy holds the greatest abundance and diversity; the floor is dim and comparatively sparse.
'Rainforest and jungle are the same everywhere' — the structured layers create very different living conditions within one forest.
'Rainforests are hot deserts of trees' / it rains all the time — they are warm and consistently wet, but the defining traits are year-round warmth and high rainfall.
'Bright colours help animals hide' — many rainforest colours are warnings (poison) or signals, not camouflage.
'All rainforest animals live in trees' — each layer, including the floor, has its own specialised residents.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach that a tropical rainforest is not one flat scene but a vertical stack of four layers — forest floor, understory, canopy, and emergent — each with different light, food, and space, and animals whose bodies are matched to their layer. Build the layers bottom-to-top, tie each adaptation to its layer's demands, and help children reason why so many species can live in one warm, wet, year-round habitat (the most species-rich land habitat on Earth, with the canopy the richest layer — a widely taught generalisation here drawn from unverified references). Core activities centre on matching animals to layers by their adaptations; supporting activities include a labelled cross-section to explore, a predict-reveal about which layer is busiest, a categorisation/matching check, and an optional field-biologist curiosity hook.

activities.title: Stock the rainforest: match animals to their layers
feedback: When a match is correct, narrate why it works: 'The monkey's gripping tail holds on to branches as it climbs through the sunny canopy, where fruit and fresh leaves grow.'

When a mismatch is tried, show the consequence: 'On the dark floor the monkey's gripping tail has no branches to hold, and it is far from the fresh leaves and fruit growing up high — it would struggle; a tapir foraging in the litter does well here instead.'
If a child treats placement as interchangeable ('they could swap'), return to one layer's light and food and ask what that animal would eat or grip there.
activities.rationale: Layer-matching is a construction task rather than recognition: children build the adaptation→layer relationship by placing animals and reasoning about the consequence, which directly targets the 'floor is busiest' and 'animals could swap places' misconceptions. A filling 'diversity meter' as niches are correctly occupied is an optional device to make 'most species-rich' concrete.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur near the equator, are warm and wet year-round, are structured into forest floor / understory / canopy / emergent layers, and hold more species than any other land habitat, with the canopy the richest layer.
Many different kinds of living things live in different places; some organisms survive well in a given habitat — rainforest is the flagship high-diversity case.
learnerActions: Work with a vertical cross-section from the dark forest floor up to the sunlit emergent layer, with each layer labelled by its light level and food (fruit and leaves high up; litter and decomposers on the dim, damp floor).

Place animals into the layer where their body suits them: a howler monkey or prehensile-tailed creature and a sloth with hook-like claws into the canopy; a tapir, decomposers, and a ground-hunting jaguar on the forest floor; a camouflaged ambush animal such as a snake into the dim understory; a harpy eagle or large bat in the emergent layer. (Jaguars also climb into the understory, so the sim should accept that placement too.)
For each placement, say WHY the animal fits — name the adaptation (gripping tail, hooked claws, camouflage, strong flight) and the layer demand it meets.
Try a deliberate mismatch (e.g. put the gripping-tailed monkey on the floor, or the tapir up in the canopy) and describe what would go wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: An animal's body and its layer are a matched pair: adaptations such as a prehensile tail or hooked claws make an animal thrive in one layer and struggle in another. A rainforest packs in so much life precisely because its stacked layers create many different homes in one warm, wet place.

activities.title: Explore the four-layer cross-section
feedback: Prompt the child to say, for an animal they reveal, what it finds in its layer that it couldn't find elsewhere.
Reinforce that the canopy — not the floor — holds the greatest abundance and diversity (the commonly taught generalisation).
If a child thinks bright colours help animals hide, note that many rainforest colours (e.g. poison dart frogs) are warning signals, not camouflage.
activities.rationale: A rich, labelled cross-section conveys the vertical stack and light gradient well and lets a child explore structure before being asked to build it; a tap-to-reveal layer with a lift-the-flap 'why here?' card is an optional way to make exploration active. This is a scaffold for the matching task — it shows the structure but does not itself let the child test placement or its consequences.
sourceClaims: Rainforest layers extend KS1/KS2 habitat and adaptation content by showing one habitat containing many micro-environments.

Tropical rainforests occur near the equator, are warm and wet year-round, are structured into forest floor / understory / canopy / emergent layers, and hold more species than any other land habitat, with the canopy the richest layer.
Many bright rainforest colours are warning (aposematic) signals of toxicity rather than camouflage.
learnerActions: Study a tall cross-section of the rainforest built bottom-to-top: forest floor, understory, canopy, emergent.

Reveal the signature animals in each layer and, for each, a 'why here?' note linking its body to the layer (prehensile tail gripping a branch, a sloth's hook-like claws, a tree frog's sticky toe pads).
Trace the light gradient from the bright emergent top to the dark floor and connect it to why canopy life differs from floor life.
Compare a 'species pile-up' of a rainforest against another habitat (including a local temperate wood) to see the sheer difference in number of kinds of animals.
activities.intendedInsight: One habitat contains many micro-environments stacked vertically; light and food change with height, and this structure is why the rainforest supports so many kinds of life.

activities.title: Predict then reveal: which layer is busiest?
feedback: Treat a 'forest floor' prediction as the expected starting point, then use the reveal to prompt revision rather than marking it simply wrong.
Draw out that removing canopy trees removes the fruit, leaves, and space the canopy animals depend on.
If the child says the rainforest is cold or rains without ever stopping, locate the equator on a globe and establish warm and wet year-round (rain most days but warm), not cold.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain cycle directly confronts the common 'the floor is where most animals live' misconception by making the child commit before the reveal. Prompts about the toucan's food and the effect of logging push toward causal, layer-specific reasoning.
sourceClaims: Tropical rainforests occur near the equator, are warm and wet year-round, are structured into forest floor / understory / canopy / emergent layers, and hold more species than any other land habitat, with the canopy the richest layer.
learnerActions: Look at a labelled rainforest cross-section or photo and predict which layer holds the most animals, saying why BEFORE any reveal.
Compare the prediction with the answer: scientists think the canopy, not the forest floor, is home to the most kinds of rainforest animals.

Discuss why the canopy is richest — bright light, fruit, and leaves up top — and why the floor is dim, with fewer plants growing and fewer kinds of animals, even though it is busy with decomposers and insects.
Answer follow-up prompts: 'What does a toucan find high up that it couldn't find on the floor?' and 'If all the tall canopy trees were cut down, what would happen to the toucan?'
activities.intendedInsight: Most children expect the floor to be busiest; surfacing and then revising that prediction makes the canopy's richness and its dependence on light and food memorable.

activities.title: Sort and match check
feedback: For a sorting error, revisit that layer's light and food and ask which animal body features would help there.
For the species-richness question, reinforce the combination of warmth, constant moisture, and many layered niches.
Flag the 'bright colours = hiding' choice and correct it to warning signals where relevant.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and adaptation-matching can check classification directly and surface the 'floor is busiest' and 'bright = hiding' errors. A sort checks rather than builds the layer intuition and does not by itself elicit the child's full explanation, so it is best used after the matching and exploration activities.
sourceClaims: Many different kinds of living things live in different places; some organisms survive well in a given habitat — rainforest is the flagship high-diversity case.
Many bright rainforest colours are warning (aposematic) signals of toxicity rather than camouflage.
learnerActions: Sort a set of rainforest animals into their correct layers.
Match adaptations to the layer demand they meet (gripping tail → canopy; camouflage and ambush → dim understory; foraging/decomposing → floor; strong flight → emergent).
Answer a short question on why rainforests hold so many species (warm, wet, year-round, many niches across stacked layers).
activities.intendedInsight: The child can categorise animals by layer and connect adaptations to layer demands, and can state why the habitat is so species-rich.

activities.title: Optional: canopy biologist curiosity hook
feedback: Use the child's questions to connect back to why the canopy — being high, bright, and fruit-rich — holds so much life.
Redirect to the cross-section if curiosity turns to how the layers themselves differ.
activities.rationale: An in-role biography can feed curiosity about how the treetops are studied. It is a motivational supplement: the conversation can spark interest but does not itself convey the vertical layer structure, which the cross-section shows directly; any comparative advantage over other media is not established by the sources.
learnerActions: Hear or read a short in-role account from a field biologist describing a canopy walkway and how scientists study the treetops.
Pose a question about how researchers reach and observe canopy animals that are hard to see from the ground.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientists study the rainforest in layers too; the hard-to-reach canopy requires special methods, which reinforces that it is a distinct, species-rich world.

constraints: Build the forest as a vertical stack bottom-to-top (floor → understory → canopy → emergent); teaching it as a flat scene loses the light-and-food-by-height idea at the heart of the topic.
Tie every adaptation to its layer's specific demand rather than listing adaptations in the abstract.
The sort/match check verifies classification but does not build the layer intuition or elicit the child's full explanation; use it after hands-on matching and exploration, not as the first encounter.
The cross-section exploration is a scaffold: it shows the layered structure but does not let the child test placements or consequences, which the matching activity provides.
The field-biologist conversation is an optional curiosity hook, not the primary means of teaching the spatial layer structure.
Keep the distinction that bright rainforest colours are often warning signals, not camouflage, so children do not generalise 'bright = hiding'.
Establish that rainforests are warm and wet year-round near the equator — not cold and not under constant non-stop storms.

Keep the jaguar consistent across activities: present it primarily as a forest-floor ground hunter (matching the assessment) while allowing the understory, and never mark one of these defensible placements wrong.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim entries remain marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The claim that the canopy is the richest rainforest layer is widely cited but the original sources are listed as unverified; 'canopy holds the majority of rainforest life' is presented as the commonly taught generalisation.

The 'diversity meter', tap-to-reveal, lift-the-flap, and drag-to-place devices are retained as optional interaction examples, not mandatory mechanisms. A 3D fly-through of the layers could convey scale and light but is a nice-to-have, not needed for the core adaptation/layer logic.

Legacy material asserted 3D 'adds nothing to the core logic' and that spatial content is 'better shown than talked through'; these comparative claims are not established by the sources and have been rendered as affordance/limit statements (including in the cross-section and conversation rationales) rather than universal claims.

The original is internally inconsistent about the jaguar: the pedagogy places it in the understory ('jaguars climbing') while the assessment treats it as a forest-floor ground hunter. Both are ecologically defensible. To prevent a learner-facing contradiction with the predict-reveal and diagnostic tasks, the matching sim now treats the floor as the jaguar's primary placement and also accepts the understory; the exact canonical layer is left to the source.

assess.poeTask: Show a labelled rainforest cross-section (or photo). Ask the child to predict which layer holds the most animals and to say why BEFORE revealing. Most children pick the forest floor; reveal that the canopy holds the majority of rainforest life — then discuss why (light, fruit, leaves up top).
probeDeeper: You said the toucan lives high up. What does it find up there that it couldn't find on the floor?
If we cut down all the tall canopy trees, what would happen to the toucan?
Rainforests have more kinds of animals than almost anywhere on Earth. Why do you think so many different animals can live in one forest?
Is a rainforest hot or cold? How do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: The rainforest has layers with different conditions. The canopy at the top is bright and full of fruit, leaves and most of the animals, so a fruit-eating, tree-climbing bird like the toucan lives there. The forest floor is dark, damp and open, where a big ground hunter like the jaguar can prowl and stalk prey. Different layers offer different light, food and space, so different animals are suited to each.

errorPatterns.pattern: The rainforest is the same all the way through — animals just pick a favourite tree ('they could swap places')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Revisit the four layers with a cross-section picture; walk from floor upward naming the light and food at each level before re-placing the animals.
errorPatterns.distractor: They could swap places — the rainforest is the same all the way up.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places toucan and jaguar interchangeably; cannot say how the floor differs from the canopy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rainforests are cold and it rains without stopping
errorPatterns.nextMove: Locate the equator on a globe; establish hot and wet (rain most days but warm), not cold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the rainforest as cold or under constant storm; unsure it sits near the equator.

errorPatterns.pattern: A rainforest is just like the woods near my house
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare species counts of a local wood versus a rainforest; introduce 'more kinds of animals than almost anywhere on Earth'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates local temperate woodland with a tropical rainforest; surprised by how many species it holds.

responseLevels.gap: Names a rainforest animal or two but treats the forest as one undifferentiated place; can't say why toucan and jaguar live at different heights, or thinks a rainforest is just like local woods.
responseLevels.full: Explains that layers differ in light, food and living space (bright fruit-rich canopy vs dark open floor), places a new animal in the right layer with a reason, knows rainforests are hot and wet near the equator, and that they hold more species than almost any habitat.
responseLevels.partial: Lists the layers (floor, understory, canopy) and places some animals, but describes the layers only as 'higher up' without saying how light, food and space differ, so can't fully explain why each animal fits its layer or place a new animal.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two rainforest animals: a toucan and a jaguar. The toucan spends its days high up in the treetops; the jaguar lives down on the forest floor. Why don't they just live in the same place? What is different about the top of the rainforest and the bottom?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who only knows 'animals live in the rainforest' says the two could live anywhere or 'they just like different trees' — no account of why each fits its height. A child who grasps layering names the difference in light, food and space between canopy and floor. Because the second tier demands a specific reason each animal matches its layer, it is hard to be right for the wrong reason.
